read.sections.0.heading.source: Spending now and saving for later
read.sections.0.heading.back: Spending now and saving for later

read.sections.0.text.note: 'Chi tiêu' (spend) and 'tiết kiệm' (save) are the chosen glossary words. 'một thứ khác'/'những thứ khác' for 'other resources' (not 'tài nguyên', which KEY_TERMS reserves for Lesson 20). Check the long sentence about the savings group.
read.sections.0.text.source: Some choices affect only today, but others affect what we can do later. To spend means to use money or another resource to get something now, such as food or a bus ride. Spending is not bad, because everyone needs some things now. To save means to keep some money or resources for later. Saving is hard when there is not much, but small amounts can add up over time. Sami puts a few coins in a tin at home until he has enough for a notebook. In some communities, neighbours save together in a group. Each person puts a small amount into the group every week, and each week one person takes it all.
read.sections.0.text.back: Some choices affect only today, but some affect what we can do later. To spend means to use money or something else to get something right now, like food or a bus ride. Spending is not bad, because everyone needs some things right now. To save means to keep back a little money or other things for later. Saving is very hard when you have little, but small amounts can add up over time. Sami puts a few coins into a tin box at home until there is enough to buy a notebook. In some communities, neighbours save together in a group. Every week, each person contributes a small amount to the group, and every week one person receives all the money.

read.sections.0.simpler.back: There are choices for today. There are choices for later. To spend is to use money or things right now. Everyone needs to spend on some things, like food. read.sections.1.text.note: 'Ngân sách' (budget) for money AND time: 'ngân sách thời gian' is understandable but slightly unusual. Alternative: 'kế hoạch thời gian'. 'chi phí cơ hội' for opportunity cost (not a glossary word, explained in the next sentences). Mei is repeated by name instead of a pronoun to avoid confusion with the learner 'bạn'.
read.sections.1.text.source: A budget is a plan for how to use money or time. It helps you compare what you have with what you need and want. Budgets are not only for money. Mei makes a time budget for her evenings. She plans time to help with dinner, to rest and to read English for 15 minutes. Budgeting is really about choices, and every choice has an opportunity cost. If Mei reads for 15 minutes, she has 15 fewer minutes for games on the shared phone. This is a trade-off: giving up one thing to get another. A careful budget helps you see your trade-offs before you choose.
read.sections.1.text.back: A budget is a plan for how to use money or time. It helps you compare what you have with what you need and want. A budget is not only for money. Mei makes a time budget for her evenings. Mei plans time to help prepare dinner, to rest and to read English for 15 minutes. Budgeting is really about choices, and every choice has an opportunity cost. If Mei reads for 15 minutes, Mei will have 15 minutes less to play games on the shared phone. This is a trade-off: giving up one thing to get another. A careful budget helps you see your trade-offs before you choose.

read.sections.2.text.source: A goal is something you want to do or get, and you work towards it step by step. Nobody can control everything about the future, and plans can change when things around us change. That is why small, short goals are useful. They are goals you can work on now, such as learning 10 new English words a week, practising a skill or staying healthy. A strong plan is also flexible. Mei's Plan A is to read every evening. Her Plan B is to read at lunchtime if the evening gets busy. A flexible plan still works when life changes.
read.sections.2.text.back: A goal is something you want to do or to have, and you try to reach it step by step. No one controls everything about the future, and plans can change when things around us change. So small, short goals are useful. These are goals you can start on right now, like learning 10 new English words each week, practising a skill or looking after your health. A good plan must also be flexible. Mei's Plan A is to read every evening. Mei's Plan B is to read at lunchtime if the evening is busy. A flexible plan can still be used when life changes.

watch.summary.source: This short video for younger learners explains spending and saving. People use money to get the things they need and want. But no one can have everything they want. This is called scarcity, so people must make choices. People usually get what they need before what they want. For example, the speaker needs a healthy lunch but wants a cupcake. So lunch comes first. Then the speaker checks if there is money left for the cupcake. When you spend, you get something now. But it may be small, and you may have little money left. When you save, you have to wait, and that can be hard. But later you can get something that costs more. There is no one right answer. Think about the good and bad sides of each choice.
watch.summary.back: This short video is for younger learners and explains spending and saving. People use money to get the things they need and want. But no one can have everything they want. This is called scarcity, so people must choose. Often people get what they need before what they want. For example, the speaker needs a healthy lunch but wants a cupcake. So lunch is put first. Then the speaker sees whether there is money left to buy the cupcake. When you spend, you get something right now. But it may be small, and you may have little money left. When you save, you have to wait, and that can be hard. But later you may be able to get something more expensive. There is no single right answer. Think about the good side and bad side of each choice.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: The lesson avoids pay, bank accounts, loans and long career plans on purpose. Keep discussion to small, short goals that learners can control. Do not ask learners where they will live in future or about their household's money. If a learner finds talk about the future upsetting, return to the small goals in the lesson and do not press.
sensitiveNotes.0.back: The lesson deliberately avoids talking about wages, bank accounts, loans and long-term career plans. Keep the discussion on small, short goals that learners can control themselves. Do not ask learners where they will live later, or ask about their family's money. If a learner feels sad talking about the future, go back to the small goals in the lesson and do not force it.

educatorNotes.0.source: The Friday savings group is a rotating savings group.
